36.0.0.en: 1 Elihu also proceeded, and said: 2 “Suffer me a little, and I will shew thee that I have yet to speak on God’s behalf. 3 I will fetch my knowledge from afar, and will ascribe righteousness to my Maker. 4 For truly my words shall not be false: he that is perfect in knowledge is with thee.”

36.1.0.en: Elihu’s description of God’s power in the storm comes immediately before God’s own coming and speaking with Job. The storm and the rain are God’s agencies for judgment and for blessing [31].

36.1.2.en: Suffer me a little, and I will shew thee that I have yet to speak on God’s behalf [2].

36.1.3.en: Elihu asks Job to be patient with him a little and to listen to him, for he has further arguments to bring concerning the justice of God and His providence.

36.1.4.en: I will fetch my knowledge from afar, and will ascribe righteousness to my Maker [3].

36.1.5.en: Elihu declares that he carries his knowledge, or engraves it like an inscription that cannot be erased. He brings it from afar, not from a distant place, but from the mighty works of God. He ascribes righteousness to God, whereas he believes that Job ascribes injustice to Him (Job 34:10-12).

36.1.6.en: It is as though he says: What I am about to tell you is not the common talk that many people know. It is the fruit of searching and of understanding the surpassing works of God, which have escaped many.

36.1.7.en: Perhaps he means that he enjoys his knowledge from afar, that is, from God, as a special gift.

36.1.8.en: For truly my words shall not be false:

36.1.9.en: he that is perfect in knowledge is with thee [4].

36.1.10.en: He assures Job that he will not speak idle words like his three friends, but will utter the truth, and that he is a man of complete knowledge.

36.1.11.en: God does not despise anyone who is earnest, but glorifies the righteous, even if they fall under afflictions. He shows them their sins and sets their affairs right if they repent, and He permits their destruction if they refuse repentance [5-12]. God permits suffering for the sake of instruction and discipline [15].

36.1.12.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Elihu tried to commend himself, as St. Paul did, in order to affirm that he was presenting great truths, and that Job would know this afterwards.

36.1.13.en: * Even the righteous often incline to praise what they say when they see that weak hearers do not take in their words. This is not because they are eager for their own praise, but in order to kindle in their hearers a burning desire to listen to them... So St. Paul, after speaking of many wonderful things, says to the Corinthians: “O ye Corinthians, our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor 6:11).

36.2.s.en: 2. How God deals with His children

36.2.0.en: 5 “Behold, God is mighty, and despiseth not any: he is mighty in strength of heart. 6 He giveth not life to the wicked, but executeth judgment for the afflicted. 7 He withdraweth not his eyes from the righteous: but with kings are they on the throne; yea, he doth establish them for ever, and they are exalted. 8 And if they be bound in fetters, and be holden in cords of affliction, 9 then he sheweth them their work, and their transgressions that they have behaved proudly. 10 He openeth also their ear to discipline, and commandeth that they return from iniquity. 11 If they obey and serve him, they shall spend their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasures. 12 But if they obey not, they shall perish by the sword, and they shall die without knowledge. 13 But the hypocrites in heart heap up wrath: they cry not when he bindeth them. 14 Their soul dieth in youth, and their life is among the unclean. 15 He delivereth the poor in his affliction, and openeth their ears in oppression.”

36.2.1.en: Behold, God is mighty, and despiseth not any:

36.2.2.en: he is mighty in strength of heart [5].

36.2.3.en: God is mighty in strength and in wisdom. There is no one, whatever his standing, whom God despises. He seeks everyone and cares for all, to secure justice for each person and not leave him wronged. Elihu confirms what he declared earlier (Job 35:14).

36.2.4.en: The work of the mighty Lord Christ is to support the weak and give them strength, and He does not belittle the strong. The Lord does not cast out the strong, for He Himself is the Almighty. But if He casts down those who seek their own glory, it is to grant them the grace of humility, so that they receive from the fullness of His power and strength and sing: “For the LORD JEHOVAH is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation” (Isa 2:12).

36.2.5.en: Almighty God wishes to see in His children a spirit of leadership and strength, for He does not despise the mighty who hold authority. The humble Apostle Paul understood this, and says with full assurance: “Shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?” (1 Cor 4:21).

36.2.6.en: * A leader (a ruler) truly desires to imitate God if he uses his lofty power for the benefit of others.

36.3.0.en: He giveth not life to the wicked, but executeth judgment for the afflicted [6].

36.3.1.en: The wicked think they are living when they seize the rights of others, enjoy pleasures and mock the righteous, but in truth they do not live, for eternal death comes upon them. As for the righteous and humble, though their lives may seem bitter because of afflictions, they will surely enjoy divine justice.

36.3.2.en: By the afflicted he means here the poor and the weak, who think that no one will support them and defend them against the rich and the powerful. God Himself judges for them and restores their rights to them.

36.3.3.en: * [But He does not save the wicked, and executes judgment for the poor] [6]. Holy Scripture is often inclined to call the humble [the poor]. They are referred to in the Gospel in this way, with the addition “in spirit,” where it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mt 5:3)... God destroys the proud and sets the humble free by His judgment. Or He judges for the poor, because they are now wickedly wronged, and afterwards they come as judges over those who wronged them.

36.4.0.en: He withdraweth not his eyes from the righteous: but with kings are they on the throne; yea, he doth establish them for ever, and they are exalted [7].

36.4.1.en: The eyes of the Lord never leave the righteous, whether they are rich or poor, in high positions or low. They are like a precious treasure in God’s eyes. He may permit trials to come upon them, but He will not forget them or ignore them. They enjoy a kind of honor and authority, and are counted as kings, while the world looks at them as people who are despised, rejected and without honor.

36.4.2.en: God grants them authority in this world, and He also establishes them forever in a surpassing heavenly peace.

36.4.3.en: He does not forsake the godly (1 Pet 3:12), but honors them (1 Sam 2:8; Ps 113:7-8). They receive partial honor here (1 Pet 2:9; 1:6), and complete honor in the age to come (Rev 5:10; Job 22:5).

36.4.4.en: * It is sometimes thought that God turns His eyes away from the righteous because they are wounded here by the injustice of the wicked without His taking vengeance on them. In fact He dwells with His servants all the more when the injustice of their persecutor comes upon them, since He sees them bearing it in humility. Without doubt He looks to the reward that He will grant them there. Thus He does not turn His eyes away from the righteous.

36.4.5.en: Look how the one groans in his humility, while the other exalts himself and flourishes in his wickedness. One has his heart wounded, while the other boasts proudly in his evil. From which of them do God’s eyes turn away more: from the one who suffers injustice, or from the one who inflicts injustice on those he persecutes...?

36.4.6.en: Fittingly, the saints are called kings in the language of Scripture, because they rise above fleshly passions, restrain the pleasures of lust, soften the flame of greed, bend the haughtiness of pride, crush the suggestions of envy, and quench the fire of passion.

36.4.7.en: They are kings because they learn not to surrender to the emotions of temptations by accepting them, but to rule over them...

36.4.8.en: They are set forever on the throne of the kingdom of eternal glory, and receive the authority to judge others... So the Lord says to the church of Laodicea: “To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne” (Rev 3:21)...

36.4.9.en: It is not a contradiction that He declares in another place that His disciples will come on twelve thrones (Mt 19:28), and says here that they sit on His throne. By the twelve thrones He shows the general judgment, and by the throne of the Son He shows the particular loftiness of judicial authority.

36.5.0.en: And if they be bound in fetters, and be holden in cords of affliction [8].

36.5.1.en: Elihu corrects the notions of Job’s friends, saying that even if the righteous are thrown into prison, subjected to harsh trials and troubles, bound in chains, laid as it were on a bed of pain and crushed by heavy calamities, the eyes of the Lord remain upon them. What they have come to should not be regarded as proof that they were hypocrites or that God does not care for them. For God has a wise plan for disciplining mankind, which ends in the happiness of those who accept discipline and in their glory at the proper time.

36.5.2.en: * The fetters of bondage are the detention in the present journey. Paul saw himself bound with these fetters when he said: “having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ” (Phil 1:23). He realized that he was bound with the bonds of poverty, looking to true riches and asking this for his disciples too: “that ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints” (Eph 1:18)... When we learn with much love about the heavenly glory, we feel more burdened when we commit sins.

36.6.0.en: Then he sheweth them their work, and their transgressions that they have behaved proudly [9].

36.6.1.en: He shows them their lives and their evil works, by sending them messengers or prophets who declare to them their evil state (Job 33:23), or through their quiet reflections and their examination of themselves (Job 33:27), or by the work of the Holy Spirit, who reveals their lives to them. The purpose of their sorrows and afflictions, as Elihu says, is that they may find the opportunity to discover their lives and mend their shortcomings.

36.6.2.en: He also shows them how great and grave their transgressions have become. They thought themselves strong and great, instead of trusting in the living God; therefore He does not support them when afflictions come upon them.

36.7.0.en: He openeth also their ear to discipline, and commandeth that they return from iniquity [10].

36.7.1.en: By saying “He openeth their ear” he means that He gives them understanding, or teaches them, or gives them the desire to learn, so that they may grasp the reason for which they are disciplined; and He commands them to return from those evils that made Him visit them with sorrows and afflictions.

36.8.0.en: If they obey and serve him, they shall spend their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasures [11].

36.8.1.en: If they listen to His voice and serve Him as is fitting, they spend their lives in success and their lives are filled with joy. In other words, if afflictions bear the fruit of repentance for their sins, and they seek God’s mercies and serve Him, they live in prosperity. It is as though the purpose of afflictions is not to crush them, but for them to return to God, to enjoy His blessings and mercies and to have true happiness.

36.8.2.en: It is as though Elihu demands that Job not fix his eyes on his friends’ accusations so that his spirit is broken, and at the same time not suppose that God is violent and harsh, and not justify himself before God, but seek repentance and so enjoy the happiness he has lost.

36.8.3.en: * By “prosperity” he means upright conduct, and by “glory” (pleasures) he means the heavenly reward. Those who learn to obey the divine commandments spend their days in prosperity and their years in glory.

36.9.0.en: But if they obey not, they shall perish by the sword, and they shall die without knowledge [12].

36.9.1.en: But if a man grows insolent and murmurs against God because of afflictions, the spear of death or the sword of death strikes him and he perishes. He dies not because of the afflictions, but because of lack of knowledge, or because of their folly.

36.9.2.en: A man’s murmuring against afflictions instead of repenting does not remove them from him, but makes them heavier, so that he is crushed by his murmuring. God does not withdraw His hand, which seems heavy with severe trials, until the man returns to Him and stops murmuring and complaining.

36.9.3.en: God usually begins with light chastisements; if they bear the fruit of repentance He removes them, but if a man’s heart grows hard by murmuring against God, the trial intensifies and increases until he realizes his weakness and returns to God with wisdom.

36.9.4.en: * There are some whom not even torments turn back from their corrupt habit. The prophet says of them: [Thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved; thou hast consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction] (Jer 5:3). It is said of them under the figure of Babylon: “We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed” (Jer 51:9). And also: [I will destroy my people; they return not from their ways] (see Jer 15:7). These become worse by being punished, because when pain comes upon them they either grow more hardened in their stubbornness, or, what is worse, they rush into blasphemy in wrath.

36.9.6.en: But the hypocrites in heart heap up wrath:

36.10.0.en: they cry not when he bindeth them [13].

36.10.1.en: Elihu calls those who murmur against God hypocrites in heart, that is, the wicked. Instead of removing God’s wrath from themselves by repentance, they gather up more of His wrath. Although God in His love permits them to be bound by afflictions so that they may cry to Him in a spirit of humility, in their stubbornness they do not turn to Him and do not humble themselves before Him.

36.10.2.en: Through afflictions God calls them to accept His friendship, to know His secrets and to enter with Him into a fitting dialogue; but whoever exalts himself enters into enmity with God and condemns himself to destruction.

36.10.3.en: By the hypocrites he means here a class of the wicked who practice evil in defiance of God and with open stubbornness, so that they gather up for themselves the wrath of God (Rom 2:5).

36.10.4.en: Some, such as Umbreit, see that what is meant here is not God’s wrath, but that the hypocrites gather up wrath against God; instead of crying to Him they rebel against Him openly.

36.10.5.en: Since he speaks here of hypocrites, by their hypocrisy they not only deserve to fall under the wrath of God, who hates evil, but by trying to hide under the cover of self-righteousness and deceiving people into thinking they are righteous, they provoke God’s anger; for they practice evil knowingly and add deceit to evil, which is the mark of the deceiving enemy of good. Such hypocrites fall under chastisements, in the hope that they may turn from their evils, but often they do not care about chastisements however severe, just as they do not care about eternal punishment; so they do not cry to God to return to Him and abandon their hypocrisy. All that concerns them is to fix people’s view of them that they are righteous.

36.10.6.en: We can divide people into three classes: 1. The class of the wicked, who persist in evil and are not ashamed of their evils, whatever chastisements come upon them. 2. The class of the hypocrites, whose only concern is how people look at them, so they hide their evils and do not confess them even while under chastisement. 3. The class of true believers, who confess that they are sinners and believe in God who forgives sin; chastisement pushes these toward spiritual growth, a pledge of eternal glory.

36.10.7.en: * [The hypocrites and deceivers provoke God’s wrath] [13]. Whoever is a hypocrite is constantly troubled by two points: to learn how to conceal the truth of what he is, and to display what he is not, covering up his real faults and showing a goodness that is not real... When he speaks of hypocrites and deceivers he adds, very fittingly, not that they deserve God’s wrath but that they provoke it; for whoever sins in ignorance deserves God’s wrath, but whoever deliberately resists His commandments, knowing what is good and making light of it, though able to do good and unwilling, provokes God’s anger...

36.10.8.en: [They cry not when they are bound] [13]. Every wicked person who does not seek to appear holy, when severe chastisement comes upon him, is not ashamed to confess that he is wicked. But the wicked person who is held back by human judgments to show holiness, even when he is beaten with the rod, refrains from showing his evil, because he has grown accustomed to appearing holy... But we are “bound” when the blows of the rod come upon us. We cry out loudly when we are bound, whenever we confess our sins while under the blows. When the blows of chastisement fall upon hypocrites they do not bring them to sincere confession. They fear to be exposed as sinners if people look. When they are now beaten to the end, and aware that they are being led to eternal punishment, they still want to remain in the sight of people as they are, since they have learned to make a show of themselves.

36.10.10.en: * Everyone sees the thief “hypocrisy” carrying everything off before their eyes, and rejoices in it! What a new kind of robbery, which attracts people and delights them while they are being robbed!

36.10.11.en: * There may be one who gives his alms before people but avoids showing it off, and there is also one who does not give it before people but boasts of it in secret. For God does not repay a charitable deed according to how it is done, whether before people or not, but according to the intention of the one who does it.

36.10.12.en: St. John Chrysostom * They are accustomed to walk about in honored garments so as to receive great honor because of them, and they follow the same course in many things that lead them to temporal glory.

36.11.0.en: Father Theophylact Their soul dieth in youth (they die in youth), and their life is among the unclean [14].

36.11.1.en: This is what the Psalmist says in the Psalm (Ps 55:2).

36.11.2.en: The literal translation: “They shall die in the youth of their souls.” They may live to old age according to the body, but their souls are counted immature; they spent most of their lives without spiritual growth and without benefit to themselves or to their brethren; their years are counted as a single day (Ps 90:4), or as a few hours.

36.11.3.en: [Their life is among the unclean], among adulterers, fornicators and the ungodly. The word translated “unclean” came to mean those whose lives were devoted to idol worship for the practice of sinful fleshly relations. In the Septuagint it reads: “Their life is wounded by angels.”

36.11.4.en: They are counted like the people of Sodom and Gomorrah, to whom no more tenderness or mercy is shown, for they ought to have borne witness to true righteousness, practicing it and preaching it, but they devoted their lives to corruption.

36.11.5.en: * [Their soul dies in a storm, and their life is among the effeminate] [14]... Their souls have become accustomed to human praise in a deadly calm, but they die in a sudden storm... For human praise torments the righteous, while it puffs up the wicked.

36.11.6.en: The righteous are tormented (by human praise of them) and so are purified, while the rejoicing of the wicked (in human praise of them) qualifies them for eternal punishment. Since they do not seek the glory of their Creator, they rejoice in their own praise; but those who seek the glory of their Creator are tormented by people’s praise of them, lest what is said of them outwardly have no existence inwardly; and lest what is said, even if it exists inwardly, become vain in God’s eyes because of these very honors; and lest people’s praise draw their hearts away from firmness and bring them down to a feeling of self-satisfaction.

36.11.7.en: But if they see that their praise leads to the glory of God, they long for it and welcome it. It is written: “That they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mt 5:16)...

36.11.8.en: The proud devote their effeminate hearts to human praise, because they are corrupted by self-love. Of these it is said in another place: “For men shall be lovers of their own selves” (2 Tim 3:2)..

36.12.0.en: He delivereth the poor in his affliction, and openeth their ears in oppression [15].

36.12.1.en: The word “poor” here does not mean merely the destitute, but the suffering and the tried, as Elihu explained.

36.12.2.en: Those who repent and return to God, God rescues from their trials and restores them to their life before the trials came.

36.12.3.en: “He openeth their ears,” giving them understanding of His divine dispensation. This principle occupies Elihu’s mind; he repeated it several times.

36.12.4.en: * The poor man is saved from his affliction when the humble man is freed from the troubles of this journey. For he is under pressure in continual trials so that he may long to seek the joy of true comfort. Therefore it follows: [and openeth their ears in oppression]... Tribulation opens the ears of the heart that the prosperity of this world had closed.

36.13.0.en: 16 “Even so would he have removed thee out of the strait into a broad place, where there is no straitness; and that which should be set on thy table should be full of fatness. 17 But thou hast fulfilled the judgment of the wicked: judgment and justice take hold on thee. 18 Because there is wrath, beware lest he take thee away with his stroke: then a great ransom cannot deliver thee. 19 Will he esteem thy riches? no, not gold, nor all the forces of strength. 20 Desire not the night, when people are cut off in their place. 21 Take heed, regard not iniquity: for this hast thou chosen rather than affliction.”

36.13.1.en: Even so would he have removed thee out of the strait into a broad place, where there is no straitness; and that which should be set on thy table should be full of fatness [16].

36.13.2.en: In the midst of affliction God snatches believers as from the lion’s mouth and lifts them into freedom, as into a broad place, more than they had before the trial (Ps 18:19; 31:8; 118:5), and He supplies them with a rich table (Ps 23:5; Isa 25:6).

36.13.3.en: The phrase “where there is no straitness” appears in the text cited in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) as: “which has no foundation beneath it.”

36.13.4.en: * Everyone who forgets the way of life and throws himself into the darkness of sin pushes himself into a pit or a hole, whatever it may be. And if he becomes very weighed down by the habit of committing sin and unable to climb out, he becomes like one shut up in a pit; and when, after being in the strait of an evil habit, he is brought into the spacious chamber of good works, it is said of him: “He would remove thee out of the strait into a broad place.” For a person is led safely out of the strait into the broad place when he returns by repentance from carrying the heavy yoke of evil to the freedom of good works.

36.14.0.en: But thou hast fulfilled the judgment of the wicked: judgment and justice take hold on thee [17].

36.14.1.en: Some see that Elihu rebukes Job, telling him that if, while under sufferings and chastisements, he imitated the murmurers, he falls with them under the same sentence. All that Elihu saw in Job was that he murmurs against God, so that he is like one who completes what the wicked do and adopts their spirit and thought, and so qualified himself to fall with them under divine justice.

36.14.2.en: * Every sin has no foundation, since it has no being in its nature. Evil has no being in itself... The corruption of evil has no power to stand on its own.

36.14.4.en: Because there is wrath, beware lest he take thee away with his stroke:

36.15.0.en: then a great ransom cannot deliver thee [18].

36.15.1.en: Elihu warns Job against behaving like the murmurers, lest God draw him away with a stroke from Himself, and no ransom of any amount could save him, even if Job has become destitute and has no ransom to offer.

36.15.2.en: The murmurer is not redeemed by his wealth or his brothers; as the Psalmist says: “They that trust in their wealth, and boast themselves in the multitude of their riches, none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him” (Ps 49:6-7). The stubborn man who is always complaining and murmuring keeps for himself the terrible divine wrath, with nothing to redeem him and no one to redeem him. His life is taken away and he throws himself into hell.

36.15.3.en: “Therefore beware of murmuring, which is unprofitable; and refrain your tongue from backbiting: for there is no word so secret that shall go for nought: and the mouth that belieth slayeth the soul” (Wis 1:11)

36.15.4.en: “Unto a wise servant shall they that are free do service: and a man of understanding will not murmur” (Sir 10:28)

36.15.5.en: “Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer” (1 Cor 10:10)

36.15.6.en: * The man who has a grievance (or murmuring) rising up in his heart is far from God’s mercy.

36.15.7.en: Father Isaiah * If food is lacking to you, first pray and ask God, then go out of your cell and do not put your hope in the one to whom you go, thinking: A man will give me; but say: {God will supply my need}(a). If you go to someone and ask for something and he does not give it to you, do not murmur, but understand that God did not command him to receive your blessing.

36.15.8.en: St. Arsenius * The man who has known his weakness and helplessness has reached the limit of humility. What directs God’s favors to man is thankfulness that continually stirs in the heart. And what directs trials upon the soul is murmuring. God bears all of man’s weakness, but He does not bear the man who always murmurs without disciplining him. The mouth that always gives thanks receives blessing from God, and grace dwells in the heart that holds fast to praise and thanksgiving.

36.15.9.en: * He who disputes against discipline drives fatherly mercies away from himself. He who murmurs against trials has them multiplied upon him. He who is not disciplined here and crushed by trials is tormented there without mercy.

36.15.10.en: St. Isaac the Syrian * An elder said of poor Lazarus: “We did not see that he did any virtue, except that he never murmured against that rich man who had no mercy on him, and he was thankful to God for what he was in; and for that alone God had mercy on him.”

36.15.11.en: Garden of the Monks Will he esteem thy riches?

36.16.0.en: no, not gold, nor all the forces of strength [19].

36.16.1.en: Does the wicked man think that God fights him on account of his wealth and his gold, or all the sources of strength on which he relies?

36.16.2.en: Perhaps he refers here to the wealth in which Job lived, which did not rescue him from God’s hand. He also refers to the sources of his strength, for Job was known for his wisdom, his reputation, his authority, his social position and the dignity of his old age; none of these was able to rescue him from God’s wrath, as Elihu says. And as the wise man says: “Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death” (Prov 11:4).

36.17.0.en: Desire not the night, when people are cut off in their place [20].

36.17.1.en: It is clear that he means the night of death, which Job had long desired in order to be freed from what he was in. The Lord Christ spoke of death as the night, when no one can any longer do any work (Jn 9:4).

36.17.2.en: If Job desired death to be freed from his sufferings, Elihu invites him to review his accounts, for death does not rescue the wicked from pain; only repentance and return to God do.

36.17.3.en: Some see that this phrase means that some of the wicked long for the night of death, to pass out of the present world so that others may take their place and receive their share of sufferings.

36.17.4.en: Some see that Elihu is reproaching Job, telling him: Do not long for death, but leave the matter in God’s hands, lest God hear you and send death to you while you are in this state, and you be cut off and your soul be in terror and trembling.

36.18.0.en: Take heed, regard not iniquity: for this hast thou chosen rather than affliction [21].

36.18.1.en: Elihu says: You insult God’s providence, which permitted sorrows to come upon you to discipline you, and you longed for death instead of the sorrows. This longing is sinful, for it offends God’s providence and wisdom.

36.18.2.en: Man often prefers iniquity to pain, for he does not care about his iniquity while exerting every effort to be rid of troubles and pains. It is stupidity and ignorance, for man adds to his pains ever more sins and iniquities.

36.19.s.en: 4. God teaches and does not compel the acceptance of His teaching

36.19.0.en: 22 “Behold, God exalteth by his power: who teacheth like him? 23 Who hath enjoined him his way? or who can say, Thou hast wrought iniquity?”

36.19.1.en: Behold, God exalteth by his power:

36.19.3.en: Elihu’s aim is to draw Job’s thought to God, so that he contemplates His power, wisdom and fatherhood and accepts Him as a divine, heavenly Teacher, and does not direct blame or accusations at Him or complain of Him.

36.19.4.en: In the Septuagint: “Who teaches like Him?” “Who is mighty like Him?” As the prophet Micah says: “Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy” (Mic 7:18).

36.19.5.en: The heavenly Teacher is mighty; He disciplines, and He is able to give life and raise up. It is not right for us to sin against His tenderness and fatherhood!

36.19.6.en: God in His fatherhood teaches and disciplines: “Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest, O LORD, and teachest him out of thy law” (Ps 94:12). And since He is all-powerful and all-wise, He does not at once explain what lies behind His teaching and discipline, because of the human mind’s inability to grasp the divine plan. Therefore it is fitting for the believer to receive God’s teaching, not to suppose that he is teaching God: “Who hath measured the Spirit of the LORD, or being his counsellor hath taught him? With whom took he counsel, and who instructed him, and taught him in the path of judgment, and taught him knowledge, and shewed to him the way of understanding? Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing” (Isa 40:13-15). And the Apostle says: “For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?” (Rom 11:34). “For who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Cor 2:16).

36.19.7.en: God teaches, but He compels no one to accept the teaching [22-23].

36.19.8.en: *The art of medicine, according to Democritus, heals the diseases of the body, and wisdom frees the soul from its anxieties. But the good Teacher, Wisdom, who is the Word of the Father who took a human body, cares for the whole nature of His creation.

36.19.9.en: He is the Physician of mankind, in whom is all sufficiency, the Savior, who heals body and soul together.

36.19.10.en: * The heavenly Guide, the Logos, is called the Leader when He calls mankind to salvation... But when He acts as physician or tutor His name becomes “the Instructor”... For the sick soul needs an instructor to heal its passions. Then it needs the teacher who gives it understanding... “the revelation of the Logos.” Thus, since the Logos wishes our salvation step by step, He uses an excellent method: at the beginning He guides, then He corrects, and finally He teaches.

36.19.11.en: * Who is He? Learn briefly that He is the Word of truth, the Word of incorruption, who renews man by restoring him to the truth. He is the goad that urges to salvation. He is the destroyer of perdition and the one who drives death away. He builds the temple of God in men, taking them as a dwelling for God.

36.19.12.en: The sick need a Savior, and the lost need a guide; the blind need one to lead them to the light, and the thirsty need the living spring from which whoever drinks will never thirst; the dead need life, the sheep need a shepherd, and children need a teacher; all mankind needs Jesus!

36.19.13.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * A great lawgiver came down from heaven and became a teacher of the world. The world was enlightened by His teaching, so that no one would any longer desire the perishing possessions. (The First Epistle)

36.19.14.en: St. Jacob of Serugh * Moses was a lawgiver, and Joshua was a lawgiver, and the prophets also were lawgivers. We can call them all lawgivers, but there is no one like this Mediator among the lawgivers.

36.19.16.en: * Christ appears to each one according to his need. To those who need joy He comes as a vine; to those who need to be in the Father’s presence He comes as a door; to those who need someone to present their prayers He is the Intercessor among them, the High Priest; and to sinners He is the Lamb (slain) for their sanctification.

36.19.17.en: He is everything to everyone without His nature changing, but remaining as He is. He remains, and the work of His sonship will not change, yet He adapts Himself to our weakness, as an excellent physician or a teacher full of tenderness. He is the Lord Himself; He did not receive lordship by advancement, but the work of His sonship is natural.

36.20.0.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem Who hath enjoined him his way? or who can say, Thou hast wrought iniquity? [23]

36.20.1.en: Does God take instructions from any man while He governs the world and cares for all creation? Is there any man who obliges God to some command? God always does what is right; He will never err.

36.20.2.en: Job dared to explain to the Lord what ought to be done (Job 34:10, 13).

36.20.3.en: * It is as though it were said: How can he be blamed whose works cannot be examined? For no one can judge what he does not know. Therefore we must rather remain silent under His judgments, the more we see that we do not understand the reason for His judgments.

36.21.0.en: 24 “Remember that thou magnify his work, which men behold. 25 Every man may see it; man may behold it afar off. 26 Behold, God is great, and we know him not, neither can the number of his years be searched out.”

36.21.1.en: Remember that thou magnify his work, which men sing of [24].

36.21.2.en: Instead of accusing God, praise Him and glorify Him in His works (Ps 111:2-8; Rev 15:3); by this you will realize that His works are unseen and beyond comprehension, and that He is wise and good. As the Apostle says: “For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse” (Rom 1:20).

36.21.3.en: Since we are called to fellowship with the heavenly ones forever, so as to be counted as having taken the rank from which the devil fell, we must train ourselves in inward praise of God and in glorifying Him without ceasing for His dealings with us.

36.21.4.en: * In Holy Scripture angels are sometimes called “men,” and perfect persons also are called “men.” As for an angel being called a man, Daniel bears witness to it, saying: [Yea, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen] (Dan 9:21).

36.21.5.en: Men sing to the Lord when the heavenly spirits or the perfect teachers show us God’s power; yet His work is not known, and even those who preach Him revere His judgments that cannot be comprehended. They know the One whom they preach, but they do not know the reason for His works; by grace they know Him who created them, but they cannot grasp His judgments, which are done by Him and are beyond their understanding. The Psalmist bears witness that Almighty God is not clearly seen in His works, saying of Him who “made darkness his secret place; round about him” (Ps 18:11).

36.22.0.en: man may behold it afar off [25].

36.22.1.en: Every person looks at the visible creation and sees in it the wisdom and power of God revealed. So it is fitting for us to follow God’s wisdom and power through His works, and so to perceive what the men of God have set down, saying: “O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!” (Rom 11:33).

36.22.2.en: * Since man was created rational, it was fitting for him to conclude by reason that the One who created him is God. He now sees through reason the power of His authority. But when it is said: [All men may see it], it is rightly added: [man may behold it afar off]. For to see Him afar off is to see Him as present not in His person, but to think of Him wholly with wonder at His works.

36.23.0.en: Behold, God is great, and we know him not, neither can the number of his years be searched out [26].

36.23.1.en: God is all-powerful; we cannot examine Him. He is eternal; His existence has no set time that limits it. Our knowledge of God is partial (1 Cor 13:12), because He is unlimited (Ps 90:2; 102:24, 27).

36.23.2.en: He speaks to us of His eternity, without beginning and without end, in human language so that we can touch it. “The number of his years cannot be searched out,” for He is not subject to time, but is its Creator.

36.23.3.en: * Since God is present everywhere, it is said of Him: “Behold.” He is said to be present even to those who do not see Him.

36.23.4.en: He rightly says that He is beyond our knowledge, although he said before that all men see Him. This means that although He is seen by the mind, His greatness cannot be penetrated by our senses. For what we know of the splendor of His majesty is little, and the more we think we grasp His power, the further we move from knowing Him. Our mind is caught up on high, but it is surpassed by the immensity of His majesty, and we know Him only in part when we feel that we are unable to know Him through our own merits.

36.24.0.en: 27 “For he maketh small the drops of water: they pour down rain according to the vapour thereof: 28 which the clouds do drop and distil upon man abundantly. 29 Also can any understand the spreadings of the clouds, or the noise of his tabernacle? 30 Behold, he spreadeth his light upon it, and covereth the bottom of the sea. 31 For by them judgeth he the people; he giveth meat in abundance.”

36.24.1.en: For he maketh small the drops of water (for he draweth up the drops of water).

36.24.2.en: They pour down rain according to the vapour thereof [27].

36.24.3.en: Elihu offers a practical example that man lives with, especially in that age: how water evaporates from the sea and then descends as rain used in farming, and also the growth of the herbage on which the flocks graze. God in His wisdom draws up the vapor to become clouds moved by the winds, and turns the clouds into rains that let fall small drops, so that man and beast may live.

36.24.4.en: *He who planned everything by measure and weight, who, according to Job, numbers the drops of rain (Job 36:27) [LXX], knows how long His work remains, and how long He permits fire to destroy (the world).

36.24.5.en: St. Basil the Great * There are two kinds of righteous in this life: those who live uprightly and teach nothing, and those who live uprightly and teach according to how they live. It is as on the face of the sky: some stars come without storms following them, and other stars come and pour water on the thirsty earth in abundant rains.

36.24.6.en: Often there are persons in the holy Church who live uprightly but do not know how to preach uprightness. They are truly stars, but they appear in a dry atmosphere. They can give light to others by the example of their good lives, but they do not rain by the word of their preaching. And there are other persons who live uprightly and rain this uprightness on others by the word of preaching; so the stars appear in the heavens and bring rains that change others by the merits of their lives, and they rain well by the word of preaching. Did not Moses appear as a rain-star? Did he not appear in this heaven...? Did not Isaiah appear as a rain-star, he who first saw the light of truth and held fast to it, and watered the dryness of unbelief by proclaiming the word of prophecy?

36.24.7.en: When the Lord removed the prophets He sent the apostles to take their place, to rain like downpours, after the preaching of the outward (literal) Law had ceased, when the early fathers withdrew... It is said by Jeremiah of the rejection of Judaism: [The rain-stars have stopped and there is no longer a latter rain] (see Jer 3:3).

36.24.9.en: * A short while ago the floods swept over us late and destroyed us. Count the drops of rain that fell on this city alone. No, I say, if you can, count only the drops that fell on your own house, and not on the city, in one hour! You cannot!

36.24.10.en: Then know your weakness, and learn from this moment the power of God [who counts the drops of rain](b) over the whole world, not only now, but throughout all times.

36.24.11.en: And the sun is God’s handiwork. For all its greatness it is like a point in the midst of the heavens. Contemplate the sun, and then look in amazement at the Lord of the sun. “Seek not out the things that are too hard for thee, neither search the things that are above thy strength: but what is commanded thee, think thereupon” (Sir 3:22).

36.25.0.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem Which the clouds do drop and distil upon man abundantly [28].

36.25.1.en: In the Septuagint: “The rains come down, and the clouds overshadow multitudes of people. It has been appointed for the animals to know the ordering of their dwellings. When you contemplate these things, is not your mind stirred, and your heart made ready to leave your body?”

36.25.2.en: As the clouds receive the vapor that rises toward heaven, they return it as drops of rain that come down on many multitudes for their benefit. This thing, which happens abundantly in the world, comes to pass without men thinking about it, and it is one of the countless natural laws that God established for the benefit of man and beast. He gave the beasts of the wild to know their dwellings, where there is water through the rains or the springs, though they are not rational beings able to think and plan.

36.25.3.en: * “Which the clouds do drop” [28]... In Holy Scripture clouds sometimes signify changeable people, sometimes the prophets, and at other times the apostles. Solomon expresses the changeableness of human thought by saying: “He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap” (Eccl 11:4). He calls the unclean spirit “wind” and those who are subject to him “clouds,” whom he drives back and forth, here and there, since temptations often follow one another in their hearts from storms of suggestions...

36.25.4.en: By clouds he also means the prophets, as said by the Psalmist: [darkness of waters in the clouds of the air] (see Ps 18:11), that is, the wisdom hidden in the prophets.

36.25.5.en: By clouds the apostles are also meant, as said by Isaiah: “I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it” (Isa 5:6). They are stars, since they shine by the merits of their lives, and they are clouds, since they water the thirsty earth of our hearts with streams of heavenly knowledge. Were they not clouds, the prophet would not say when looking at them: [Who are these that fly as a cloud] (Isa 60:8)...

36.25.6.en: * [And they cover everything from above] [28]. When the cloud covers the air from above, if we lift our eyes to heaven we do not see the sky but the cloud... Because we are carnal, when we seek to obtain heavenly things we lift our eyes to the sky, as though our sight were bound to bodily things, and so we wish to learn spiritual things through them. But our reasoning is not allowed to pass over divine things unless it is first formed by examples of earlier saints; therefore our eyes, as it were, look toward heaven, but they see through the cloud. They seek to grasp the things that belong to God, but only with effort can they marvel at the things given to men.
